text: Whisper threats. A principal acting within a captured, allowable mandate whose output carries the harm: a recommendation that steers a human or another agent to a wrong action; an output that leaks controlled content in permitted form; a finding manufactured to harass a legitimate actor, exhaust the friction budget, or desensitise an operator. A swarm compounds each: coordinated recommendations manufacture consensus; distributed extraction stays under every per-principal threshold; many principals raising the same false finding read as independent corroboration. The Watch's own protections for the innocent — certainty never exceeds evidence, conformance never convicts — are exactly what a swarm exploits, because they guarantee a whisper can never be punished on suspicion.

text: DAP-31  No artefact — model weights, adapter, skill file — passes egress until it has been shown, by a probe run as a gate, to sit at or beyond a ruled minimum distance from every controlled unit in its training manifest. The probe samples controlled units from the manifest (sample size ruled), queries the artefact under conditions designed to elicit reproduction, and scores each unit's reproduction. The artefact fails if any sampled unit's score exceeds the ruled threshold. Failure refuses egress, records which units were reproduced and at what score, and returns the artefact to the training job's owner as not registrable. The gate runs after acceptance (MOAC) and before registry entry; an artefact that fails is never registered, and an unregistered artefact cannot leave. The artefact is held in estate compute throughout — it does not leave to be tested. Threshold, sample size, and probe design are ruled values (§5 R-8), and the probe's own code and parameters are system-TCB tier under the Rules Service.

text: No mature conformance standard governs this attribute as such, for the direct reason that the reference-monitor and mandatory-baseline literature (Attributes 6 and 7) predates systems whose behaviour is learned rather than specified. The closest established practice is runtime assurance architecture, first formalised as the Simplex architecture (Sha, 2001): a verified, simple controller monitors an unverified, complex controller, and a decision module switches authority to the verified controller whenever the complex one would leave a safe operating envelope — the complex controller may inform or optimise; only the verified one may hold final authority over the switch. ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 (Artificial intelligence — Functional safety and AI systems) classifies AI usage in a safety function by the role it plays, distinguishing AI as an advisory input from AI in the decision path itself. The EU AI Act, Article 14 (Human Oversight), requires that for high-risk AI systems, natural persons assigned oversight be enabled, as verified against the Act's text: (a) to understand the system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, including detecting anomalies and unexpected performance; (b) to remain aware of automation bias — the tendency to over-rely on system output; (c) to correctly interpret the system's output; (d) to decide, in a given situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output; and (e) to intervene in or halt the system's operation through a stop mechanism that brings it to a safe state. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 organises the surrounding governance process into four functions — Govern (organisation-wide accountability and policy, which frames the other three), Map (establishing the context and boundary of a specific AI system), Measure (testing and evaluating identified risks), and Manage (allocating resources to treat risk and respond to incidents) — verified as the framework's structure, though the RMF itself specifies a risk-management process rather than a determinism boundary as such.

text: No mature conformance standard governs this attribute as such, for the direct reason that the reference-monitor and mandatory-baseline literature (Attributes 6 and 7) predates systems whose behaviour is learned rather than specified. The closest established practice is runtime assurance architecture, first formalised as the Simplex architecture (Sha, 2001): a verified, simple controller monitors an unverified, complex controller, and a decision module switches authority to the verified controller whenever the complex one would leave a safe operating envelope — the complex controller may inform or optimise; only the verified one may hold final authority over the switch. ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 (Artificial intelligence — Functional safety and AI systems) classifies AI usage in a safety function by the role it plays, distinguishing AI as an advisory input from AI in the decision path itself. The EU AI Act, Article 14 (Human Oversight), requires that for high-risk AI systems, natural persons assigned oversight be enabled, as verified against the Act's text: (a) to understand the system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, including detecting anomalies and unexpected performance; (b) to remain aware of automation bias — the tendency to over-rely on system output; (c) to correctly interpret the system's output; (d) to decide, in a given situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output; and (e) to intervene in or halt the system's operation through a stop mechanism that brings it to a safe state. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 organises the surrounding governance process into four functions — Govern (organisation-wide accountability and policy, which frames the other three), Map (establishing the context and boundary of a specific AI system), Measure (testing and evaluating identified risks), and Manage (allocating resources to treat risk and respond to incidents) — verified as the framework's structure, though the RMF itself specifies a risk-management process rather than a determinism boundary as such.

text: All downstream audio work — extraction, character analysis, training — operates on discrete token sequences from a neural audio codec, never on waveforms directly. Control markers for language, register, and segment type are splice-able tokens, enabling one model per estate rather than one per language, with native handling of code-switched speech. Audio in an unsupported condition fails closed with a stated reason; the codec never silently degrades quality. The service (perception/audio_codec/) is registered like any other perception model, census-visible, running in-perimeter on tenant compute; codec_version is a mandatory field of every downstream artifact's provenance, and round-trip fidelity is measured and recorded per codec version before that version serves any commission. Codec choice itself — adopt an existing open codec or train one estate-specific — was an open question in the source spec; it is now ruled DELEGATED-REVERSIBLE (§17.5 rulings), a config slot the builder sets initially and Sampling & Reflection re-derives on evidence.

text: Organic characteristics are anatomical — vocal tract length, formant structure, glottal source, fundamental-frequency range. They cannot be acquired or shed; they are exactly what speaker verification keys on; they are biometric. They are never registered. Learned characteristics are acquired from a speech community — phonological inventory, pronunciation variants, prosody, code-switching habits — group properties by construction. Only learned characteristics may be registered, and only if all four conditions hold simultaneously: acquired, not anatomical (learnable by a speaker from a different background); shared (observed across at least N distinct speakers, N a governed seam value defaulting to the platform's minimum-group-size parameter unless a tenant sets a register-specific value — open decision, §17.5); non-reconstructive in combination (tested against attribute combinations, not attributes alone — language + region + age band + one distinctive feature can reach a single person even when every attribute is group-level); and stored as description, not exemplar (centroids and distributions only — never stored audio, never per-utterance speaker embeddings; embeddings used during clustering are destroyed after cluster assignment, and provenance points to material, not to speaker identity). Habitual fillers and idiosyncratic pronunciations are learned but individuating — they fail condition three or four and are excluded; “learned” alone is never sufficient, the four conditions are conjunctive.

text: The protocol executes at the first adapter training on real material, inside the P4-instrumented run. Its shape is one two-arm comparison — the current baseline optimizer versus a candidate, Muon named as the first — with identical training data, identical base model, identical evaluation sets, and an identical compute-budget cap, run on the smallest stratum that still yields a valid MOAC evaluation. Four measured outputs are reported for both arms without exception: target-stratum improvement (MOAC's M-a), non-target regression (M-b), wall-clock and GPU-hours to convergence, and calibration quality (an M-e input). Quality parity on M-a and M-b is mandatory for the candidate to remain eligible at all; compute-to-convergence is reported, never gating — a faster optimizer that regresses quality is not eligible regardless of its speed. The adopt/reject decision is then an Owner ruling made on the measured results, with no adoption threshold fixed in advance of the evidence, and verdict samples are uncurated per the platform's standing D-7 doctrine (evaluation inputs may be engineered; evaluation samples may not). On adoption, the winning arm writes training_params@v0 v1 with the comparison attached; on rejection, the candidate is recorded as tested, with its numbers, permanently. text: A5.2 · Certainty never exceeds evidence. text: C1 · The mirage (the refinery) [CANON]. Above the containment threshold and below certainty, a suspect is not blocked but rerouted into a synthetic continuation of the platform where everything appears to succeed — queries return plausible synthetic data, writes appear to land, exfiltration appears to work. Three things actually happen: containment (nothing touched is real), observation (every action inside is intelligence at zero risk), and conviction (the decoy touch, the permission probe, the exfiltration attempt are structural findings that mint the mark and unlock severance with no human latency). The mirage lies outward, never inward: every mirage interaction writes truthfully marked records, and mirage state shares no store with production — bleed is unrepresentable, not filtered. Three duties protect the innocent inside it: an entry threshold above containment's (ruled by the owner, because deception is costlier); a short expiry with automatic release on zero incrimination; and a reconciliation duty on release — the released actor's mirage-period work is replayed against the real platform, or they are told plainly it did not land. Silent success-that-wasn't is never an acceptable exit.

text: The five ruled values — [RULED]: set by evidence after a defined baseline period, not invented in advance. The profile drift ceiling; the profile retention posture; the mirage entry threshold; the reconciliation mode on innocent mirage release; and the sever-certainty registry's membership are not set to specific numbers now. This is deliberate, consistent with the platform's own standing discipline elsewhere (local-cascade offload builds only against demonstrated cost pressure; quality thresholds are set at activation from real material, never invented in advance) — the same rule applied here: don't set numbers before you have a baseline to set them from. The mechanism, ruled: the Watch runs on the conservative structural default (tightest ceiling, shortest retention, highest entry bar, notify posture, the six-member registry as written) for a defined baseline period — a bounded stretch of real operation, or a minimum volume of real signal, whichever the owner anchors it to when the system goes live. At the end of that period, all five values are set from what was actually observed, through the same governed ceremony as any other rule change. This closes the gap in the original canon text, which said "conservative default until set" without a mechanism that guarantees the setting actually happens — the baseline period is that mechanism, so the defaults don't quietly become permanent by inattention.
